problem: A tap on a common word returns the first phrase gloss of the chapter that contains that word anywhere, even when the tapped occurrence is not in that phrase. Tapping de in "tres clases de salsa" (ch046) shows "La última vez gritó gol en un gol de Millonarios". Tapping Y in ch006 shows "And a parrot". authority: Run: for each token occurrence, located each chapter gloss phrase in the token stream and tested whether the tapped index falls inside it.
replacement: Pass the tapped word's position, and use a phrase gloss only when that position falls inside an occurrence of the phrase. Otherwise fall through to the single-word path.

quote: him, it; the thing that is
problem: There is no lexeme for the articles la, las, los. Tapping them gives lemma lo, "him, it; the thing that is" (los directly, la and las through the a to o guess). The most frequent word in Spanish glosses as "him" whenever the chapter has no phrase to misfire on: la 339, las 522, los 315 taps. Una and unas go to uno, "one", which is merely weak.
authority: Run: Bundle.gloss("la"), gloss("las"), gloss("los"); graph has l:el and l:un but no l:la, l:los, l:las, l:una.
replacement: Add closed-class lexemes: la "the", los "the", las "the", una "a, an", unos and unas "some". Keep l:lo for the pronoun, and give pronoun la and las a second sense only in the chapter gloss.

problem: The loose lookup ignores accents and swaps endings with no check that the two words are related. Real results: calla and callas give "street" (la calle, 20 uses across story and bank); lentes gives "slow"; pera gives "but"; aceras gives "steel"; Cuba gives "bucket"; perdida gives "la pérdida, loss"; mama (in mamar gallo) gives "mom"; carné gives "meat"; dañó and daña give "el daño, damage"; cuántas gives "cuanto, as much as"; cuarta gives "room, bedroom"; dicha gives "saying"; arrienda, odia, engaña, insultó, clavó, choqué, reprocha give the noun. Each one shows as "X from Y", which states a false derivation as fact.
authority: Run: Bundle.gloss over 14,651 distinct story and bank tokens; 588 fell through to looseLemma.
replacement: Remove the accent-blind step and the a to o swap for anything but known adjectives. Showing "No note for this word yet" is better than a wrong derivation. Add a verb lexeme where the noun is catching verb forms: dañar, callar, arrendar, odiar, engañar.

authority: Run through checkTurn in app/src/ui/session/scene.ts with the real scene file. Script over all containsWord, containsAny and regex constraints holding a number word and no digit.
replacement: {"type":"regex","pattern":"\\b(once|11)\\b","label":"the street: calle once"}

problem: JavaScript \b and \w are ASCII, so they break on every accented letter and on ñ. An alternative ending in an accented letter before \b can never match before a space. \w+ stops at á, é, í, ó, ú, ñ. Comparing each regex with a Unicode-aware copy over 81,784 real course sentences, 148 of 1,955 regex constraints differ. Refused today, with the label's own example among them: me enteré and se enteró (w-u38-09), se realizó (w-u38-10), me dormí and me quedé (w-u30-07, w-u31-04), se volvió and se quedó (w-u30-06), la pasé (w-u26-07), me pidió que (w-u41-01), estrené and estrenó (w-u41-09), se duplicó (w-u45-06), me entró (w-u57-12), no debí (w-u57-01), para mí (w-u10-04, w-u15-13, w-u15-14), no sé (w-u19-04), quizá (w-u29-05), Íbamos a (w-u31-10), tan rápido como and tan tímida como (w-u24-07, sc-u24-f t4), Si Tomás hubiera (w-u43-03), A Simón le gusta (w-u10-11), No es que esté (w-u46-07), bañando and soñando (w-u08-07, w-u26-01). Worst case: w-u57-12 passes the misspelt "me entro" and fails "me entró". In scenes the same fault refuses "café" in sc-u43-a t5 and "se me partió" in sc-u57-a t1.
authority: ECMAScript RegExp: \b and \w use the ASCII word set, even with the u flag. Run: scratch harness comparing both forms over bank, accepts and models; checkWriting on each sentence above.

problem: avoidsAny is a substring test on accentless text. The word tú is in 52 constraints, so it fires on any "tu" inside a word: turistas, estuvo, tuve, situación, futuro, natural, cultura, costumbre, estudiantes. "Don Hernando, me parece buena idea para los turistas" is marked as using tú (w-u15-09), and in scenes "Gracias a usted. Estuvo muy bien." is refused (sc-u45-c t5), as is "un tinto natural" (sc-u06-b t6, word tu). estás loses its accent, so it fires on estas: "hablar de estas cartas" fails w-u31-03. vas fires on nuevas (w-u28-01), ves on jueves (sc-u28-d t1), eres on mujeres.
authority: Run: checkWriting and checkTurn on the sentences above; count of avoidsAny words over all scenes and tasks.
replacement:
const toks = ` ${analysis.tokens.map((t) => t.toLowerCase()).join(' ')} `;
const bad = c.words.filter((w) => toks.includes(` ${w.trim().toLowerCase()} `));

problem: A clitic may not stand between que and the verb, and plurals and second person fail. "Me pidió que lo llamara", the label's own verb, is refused, as are "que le guardara", "que vinieran", "que fueras". The model passes only on "que no cerrara". The Unicode fix does not cure this.
authority: Run: checkWriting.
replacement: \bque\s+(no\s+)?((me|te|se|le|les|lo|la|los|las|nos)\s+)*\w+(ara|iera|era)(n|s)?\b

problem: The comment says "Estoy cansada" is just as right as "Estoy cansado" when the English does not say who speaks. That holds only when the first verb of the row is the copula. In 181 of 325 first-person rows tested, the other gender is refused with "Check the ending". Examples: u02-0257 "Tengo veinte años y estoy contento." (contenta refused), u02-0351 "Estoy enfermo, Vale.", u01-0672 "Es que estoy ocupado.", u15-0966, u33-0646, u47-0624 "Estoy demasiado cansado para salir esta noche.", u59-0958 "...y me quedé quieta." (quieto refused). A woman typing a right answer is marked wrong, and nothing in "I'm ill, Vale." tells her otherwise. About one in eight of the 181 is parser noise, so read it as about 160 rows. Listener gender has the same gap: u47-0940 "te voy a dejar sola".
authority: Run: matchTranslation with the adjective swapped, over all bank rows and turns with a first-person copula and adjective, no English gender cue and no tag.
replacement: Scan every first-person clause: for each estoy, soy, me siento, me quedé followed by an adjective, emit the other-gender variant, whatever verb comes first in the sentence.

problem: When the model is usted with no pronoun, untagged English "you" gets no tú variant, so the natural answer is refused. All 131 rows tested failed: u04-1012 "¿Quiere bolsa?" for "Do you want a bag?" refuses ¿Quieres bolsa?; u23-0820 "¿Tiene un documento de identidad?"; u02-0412 "¿Me repite, por favor?"; u37-1271 "¿Con quién quiere hablar?"; u23-0849 "¿Cuánto pagó?"; u13-0147 "¿Me da el mapa?". The Spanish cannot be guessed from the English. Plural has the same gap in rows like u36-0302 "¿Vendieron el anillo?" for "Did you sell the ring?" and u49-1006.
authority: Run: changePerson to tú, then matchTranslation, over all rows and turns with untagged "you" and a bare third-person model. A few rows are parser noise.
replacement: Treat a bare él/ella or ellos verb as usted or ustedes when the English subject is you, or add "(polite)" and "(you all)" to these rows.

problem: The bank tags usted rows "(polite)" 1,920 times and "(formal)" 308 times, but enYou knows only "(formal)". So on a "(polite)" row tú passes silently: "¿Trabajas en La Candelaria?" is marked right for "Do you work in La Candelaria? (polite)". The tag promises a register the checker does not hold the learner to. "(informal)" 315 and "(to a friend)" 6,670 are also two names for one thing.
authority: Run: matchTranslation on u01-0162; count of parenthetical tags in en.
replacement: if (/\(formal\)|\(polite\)|\bsir\b|\bmadam\b|\bma'am\b/.test(l)) return 'formal';
